doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Teaching Joe Bonamassa and goodbye
summary: He taught a young Bonamassa for a summer, then the interview ends.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Yeah. Well any students that are out there now performing that you gave some knowledge to? Any guys from Utica that sort of have made it in the biz?

Well the obvious, I had the pleasure of teaching Joe Bonamassa for a summer. And I never take any credit for his success or his ability because he did it by himself. And by the time his dad brought him to me he was like eleven years old and said “I want you to give him some direction.” After we played for ten minutes I said “he’s got his direction, we’re just going to play together.” And so he would come in and we’d jam once a week and I’d tell him how great he was and made no effort — I mean I tried to just tell him a little bit of this and a little bit of that, but you could see that he was already in the formative years and he knew what he wanted to do, and he was a very polite kid, he was very nice and treated me with a great deal of respect. But there was no way that anybody — now I’m sure he had a lot of teachers and a lot of people over the years that take credit for his ability. But it was all him. Especially — even after he got his butt kicked when Bloodline got — whatever you say — they stopped working and they lost their record deal and all this stuff, he, by himself, regrouped, got himself a little recording set-up in his bedroom and started writing, singing — he never wanted to sing a note, it was not the thing he wanted to do. He said I’ve got to learn to sing. He learned to sing, went down to New York by himself, knocking on doors, hey I was in Bloodline, I did this, I did that, looking for a producer. By the time he got to Tom Dowd, who produced the album that really did something, he did it on his own. So nobody takes credit for this man’s success. I’m proud to say I was that much in the background there, but it’s a success.
Yeah. Well, thank you for your time today. It’s been really fascinating. All right?
